It's 18 June, in Kiel. Mara, Clara's maid of honour, has slept at Clara's parents' house, by the sea. It's nine o'clock in the morning and the ceremony is at eleven.
Mara! Are you awake? I can't calm down. I'm so nervous!
Calm down. Sit down. Have a coffee first. Have you showered yet?
Yes, but I haven't washed my hair yet. And I still have to do my make-up. And get dressed. Oh God, we have to hurry!
We've got two hours. That's enough. I'll take care of your hair, your sister will take care of the make-up.
And Jonas? Is he dressed yet? Has he shaved? He always forgets something!
Jonas is at the hotel with his sisters. They're keeping an eye on him. He sent me a message: “I can't wait for today. And I've got the rings. Both of them. Not in a glove this time.”
Ha! Do you remember New Year's Eve? I was so annoyed with him back then. And at the same time I fell even more in love with him.
I remember every second. The whole hospital remembers.
Mara… How do you feel, so far away from your family? Aren't you looking forward to going home in August?
Yes, I really am. But today I don't feel far away. Today I'm exactly where I want to be. And now: sit down in front of the mirror. The bride has to make herself beautiful.
The bride is already beautiful. The bride just has to calm down.

Soft “ch” in all three: “mikh, dikh, zikh” (breathy, as in “huge”). Not “mik”!
English uses reflexives only sometimes (to wash yourself, to enjoy yourself), but many German verbs have a reflexive pronoun. Most use the pronoun in the ACCUSATIVE:
sie beeilen sich / Sie beeilen sich
Only the third person and the polite form have “sich”. The rest are the accusative pronouns you already know.

Many verbs are reflexive in German but not in English: sich beeilen (to hurry), sich ausruhen (to rest), sich erkälten (to catch a cold), sich bedanken (to say thank you!). But “to go for a walk” = spazieren gehen, NOT reflexive.
2. The dative: ich wasche MIR die Hände
When the sentence already has a direct object (usually a part of the body or an item of clothing), the reflexive pronoun changes to the DATIVE. It's only different for ich and du:
Er zieht sich die Jacke an.

In German you don't say “meine Hände” in sentences like this: “Ich wasche mir die Hände” (literally: I wash to myself the hands), not “Ich wasche meine Hände” (grammatically correct, but less natural). English says “my hands” here, German prefers “mir die Hände”.
3. The position of the reflexive pronoun
I can't wait for the wedding. (after the verb)
Today I'm especially looking forward to it. (inversion: after the pronoun subject)
Today Clara is especially looking forward to it. (with a noun: the pronoun comes before the subject!)
…, because I'm so looking forward to it. (subordinate clause)
Perfekt: reflexive verbs use HABEN: “Ich habe mich beeilt.” “Hast du dich schon angezogen?”
Ich freue mich auf den Urlaub.
I'm looking forward to the holiday. (future)
Ich freue mich über das Geschenk.
I'm pleased with the present. (present / past)
Er ärgert sich über den Zug.
He gets annoyed about the train.
Do you remember New Year's Eve?
Er hat sich in sie verliebt.
He fell in love with her.
Ich kümmere mich um die Haare.
I'll take care of the hair.
Learn the verb together with its preposition, as a single block: “sich freuen auf”. “auf” = towards the future, “über” = about something that already exists.

At half past ten everyone met in front of the old town hall in Kiel. It was a perfect June day: blue sky, a light breeze from the sea, and gulls screeching above the rooftops. The guests stood in small groups in the square, chatting: Clara's big family from Kiel, Jonas's parents and sisters from Hamburg, colleagues from ward 4 and, right at the front, a small group from Kastanienallee.

Ludwig had come with Mara and Lena by train the evening before. He had thought long and hard about whether he could manage the journey. Five hours on the train, with his back, at seventy-eight. But then he had said: “I have to see my suit dancing. Nobody's going to take that away from me.” Fritz had stayed with the Nowaks, to Kuba's delight.

Then Jonas arrived. He was wearing the navy blue suit from 1974 with the dark red tie and looked exactly as Ingrid had said fifty years ago: like a film star. Ludwig saw him coming and had to sit down on a bench. “It's just my back,” he told Lena. Lena handed him a handkerchief and said nothing.

Jonas went straight over to him. “Mr Brandt,” he said, “I've been wondering all morning whether the trousers would hold. They're holding. Mrs Hoffmann is an artist.” Then he opened his jacket a little and showed him the lining, where it said in small gold letters: “L & I 1974 · J & C 2027”. Ludwig just nodded. He couldn't speak.

At eleven the bride arrived. Clara stepped out of an old white VW Beetle that her father had been looking after in his garage for thirty years. The long silk dress moved in the wind, her red hair was put up in a bun with small white flowers in it, and on her feet, as promised, she wore comfortable flat shoes. Jonas looked at her and for a moment forgot how to breathe.

The ceremony was short and beautiful. The registrar, a friendly older lady with glasses, spoke about love and about the sea, “which is different every day and yet always stays the same sea”. When she asked Jonas whether he wanted to take Clara as his wife, he said “Yes!” so loudly that everyone laughed. Clara said it more quietly, but with tears in her eyes. Mara, who was standing next to her, handed her the ring. This time nothing fell.

Afterwards they celebrated in the big garden of Clara's parents, right on the beach. There was grilled fish, potato salad from Clara's grandmother's recipe, and a three-tier cake that Lena had baked and carried to Kiel on the train in four boxes. Clara's grandmother, a small, energetic woman of eighty, told anyone who would listen about her short red wedding dress from 1968.

In the afternoon, Mara gave a short speech as maid of honour. She had spent weeks preparing it and had practised it twenty times in front of Ludwig, who corrected her every time: “Not “ich freue mich über die Zukunft”, Mara. “Auf die Zukunft” (you're looking forward to it). The future isn't here yet!”

I've known Jonas for eight months, and Clara since a night in January, at one in the morning, in A&E. I remember it exactly: Jonas had burned his hand, Clara had frozen her hands in the snow, and the two of them had just shared the worst and the most beautiful moment of their lives. I learned a lot that night. For example, that sometimes you don't need to hurry. Some things find themselves. In a glove, for example. I'm so happy for you both. And I'm looking forward to everything that's still to come.
The guests clapped. Ludwig clapped the loudest. Lena whispered to him: “She said “auf”, Grandpa.” Ludwig nodded proudly. “Of course. She has a good teacher.”

In the evening, when the sun hung low over the sea and painted the sky orange and pink, a small band began to play. The bride and groom danced the first dance. The old navy blue suit spun round in the sand, with the dark red tie, next to a white silk dress, and Mara thought that a suit really could look happy.
After the first dance, Jonas went over to the band and had a quick word with the guitarist. Then he came over to Ludwig, who was sitting at the side with a glass of wine in his hand.
Mr Brandt, the band knows your song. The song from 1974. And Clara would like to dance with you.

Ludwig looked at him, then at Clara, who was holding out her hand to him with a smile. He slowly put his glass down on the table, stood up, much more easily than his back really allowed, and took the young bride's hand. The band played an old, slow song. A song that, more than fifty years ago, in a courtyard in Prenzlauer Berg, a young tram driver had danced to with his Ingrid.

Mara stood with Lena by the water, watching. The waves rolled gently onto the shore. Lena wiped her eyes and said: “You know, Mara, since Grandma died, Grandpa hasn't danced. Not even once.” Mara put her arm around her. The first stars appeared in the sky, and above the sea, very slowly, an old suit was dancing.
